challenges.name: single-thread-race-quiz
challenges.title: Does a single thread protect the wallet?
challenges.description: Two payment requests for the same wallet run the same async handler at the same time. Predict the outcome before you read on.

questions.explanation: Every await hands control back to the event loop. Request A reads 100,000 and waits for the database; request B runs its findById in that gap and also reads 100,000. Both pass the check and both save 20,000. Two payments are approved but only one is charged - a lost update. A single thread only guarantees that synchronous code is not interrupted; anything spanning an await can interleave.

options.text: Nothing bad: the second request waits until the first handler finishes, because Node.js is single-threaded.
Both requests can read 100,000 before either saves, so both are approved and the wallet ends at 20,000 - one debit is lost.
Node.js throws an error because two async functions modify the same object at once.
Both requests fail, because the database locks the row automatically while it is being read.

challenges.name: fix-lost-update-in-locked-debit
challenges.title: Fix the lost update inside the lock
challenges.description: The payment service wraps every debit in a per-wallet lock, yet concurrent payments still overspend. Fix debit() so the read-check-write is atomic. Hint: what does the callback passed to withLock return, and when does withLock release the lock?

tests.name: Two 80 debits on 100: only one is approved
A debit larger than the balance is rejected
Six concurrent debits drain the wallet exactly to zero

challenges.name: lock-ttl-expiry-quiz
challenges.title: What if the lock expires mid-payment?
challenges.description: Lock TTLs protect you from crashed holders - but they also mean a slow holder can lose the lock.

questions.question: Worker A takes the lock with SET lock:wallet:42 <tokenA> NX PX 3000. Its call to the payment provider stalls for 5 seconds. After 3 seconds the key expires and worker B acquires the lock with <tokenB>. When A finally finishes, it releases with a plain DEL lock:wallet:42. What is the most important consequence?
questions.explanation: A plain DEL does not check who owns the key, so A deletes B's lock while B is still mid-payment. A third request can now acquire the lock and run alongside B - mutual exclusion is gone. Release must compare the token and delete atomically (a Lua compare-and-delete), and the database write should still be guarded (fencing token or a conditional UPDATE), because an expired holder can still be running.

options.text: Nothing: DEL only removes the lock A created, so B keeps its lock.
A deletes B's lock. Another request can acquire it while B is still paying, so two payments run concurrently again.
Redis rejects the DEL because the key was re-created with a different TTL.
Redis rolls back B's payment automatically because its lock was removed.

challenges.name: redis-lock-acquire-release
challenges.title: Implement acquire/release for a Redis lock
challenges.description: Write createLock(redis) returning acquire(key, ttlMs) and release(key, token). Use SET NX PX with a fresh token per acquisition, and release only when the token still owns the lock. The in-memory redis client exposes set, get and an atomic delIfEquals (the Lua compare-and-delete).

tests.name: A held lock cannot be acquired again until it is released
Releasing with a token you do not own fails
The lock expires by itself after its TTL
An expired holder cannot release the new holder's lock
Every acquisition gets a fresh token
